notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes for **Jeremiah 14**, drawn from the sources I was able to access. I note where I could not find material on certain traditions or viewpoints.

---

## Jeremiah 14:1-6 — The Drought Described

**v. 1 — "This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought"**

- Traditional reading: The Hebrew phrase is literally "concerning the words of restraints" — a plural indicating a series of droughts, not a single event. God "restrains" the heavens from giving rain. The drought was threatened in the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:19; Deuteronomy 28:23-24). Its purpose was to bring the nation to repentance. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/ ; JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Reformed (Calvin): Calvin emphasizes that God foretold this drought so the people would know it was NOT by chance or astrology, but divine judgment. He notes the plural "restraints" — God restrains both the heavens (from rain) and the earth (from producing fruit). Men would speculate about natural causes, but the Prophet sets up "the word of Jehovah in opposition to the words of men." (Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Baptist (Garner-Howes): God sometimes withholds rain as a sign of His displeasure and as a warning of more severe judgment to follow upon the unrepentant (Deut. 28:12, 23-24; Amos 4:7-8). (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

**v. 2 — "Judah mourns and her gates languish… a cry goes up from Jerusalem"**

- Traditional: "Gates" represent the cities — the places of public gathering and justice. They "languish" because people no longer frequent them; the land is in grief. "They are black unto the ground" (KJV) indicates mourning, blackness being a sign of sorrow. The "cry" is a cry of distress going up from the whole city. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Reformed (Calvin): The gates would be reduced to solitude. The phrase "darkened to the ground" means people would be so cast down they lie in the dust, unable to raise their heads, worn down by famine. The cry ascending is evidence of despair — when hope fails, men break out into crying. (Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm)

**v. 3 — "The nobles send their servants for water… they return empty… they cover their heads"**

- Traditional: "Their little ones" (KJV) means inferiors or servants, not children. They go to cisterns (pits for collecting rainwater), but even the deepest wells are dry. Covering the head is a sign of humiliation, mourning and grief (cf. 2 Samuel 15:30). The nobles themselves are "ashamed and confounded." (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

- Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed): "On the back of that confusion came despair; 'they covered their heads.' The Orientals cover their heads when in the deepest grief, as David did… It means, 'I cannot face it. Do not look on me in my sorrow, nor expect me to look on you.'" (quoted in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

**v. 4 — "The ground is cracked because no rain has fallen… farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads"**

- Traditional: The ground is "dismayed" (literally), joining the people in horror. The plowmen cannot till the hard, cracked soil. Calvin describes the earth dissolving into dust as though pounded in a mortar. This is not a common drought but an extraordinary judgment meant to pierce the people's stupor. (Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm ; JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

**v. 5 — "Even the doe in the field deserts her newborn fawn because there is no grass"**

- Traditional: The hind (doe) is renowned for her affection toward her young, yet even she abandons her newborn because there is no grass to sustain life or produce milk. This is an extreme picture of famine reversing the natural order. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/ ; Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm)

**v. 6 — "Wild donkeys stand on barren heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail for lack of pasture"**

- Traditional: Wild donkeys are among the hardiest animals, well able to endure drought, yet even they stand on bare heights panting. "Like dragons/jackals" — JFB notes the image may refer to serpents that raise their bodies vertically to survey the area while drinking in the air with open jaws. Their eyes — normally keen for spotting water — fail them. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

- Reformed (Calvin): The wild ass can endure want for a long time, so its suffering is a sign that this drought contains "remarkable evidences of God's vengeance" far exceeding normal scarcity. The serpent-like panting pictures animals "burning with long famine." (Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm)

---

## Jeremiah 14:7-9 — Jeremiah's Intercessory Prayer

**v. 7 — "Although our iniquities testify against us, O LORD, act for the sake of Your name… our rebellions are many; we have sinned against You"**

- Traditional: Jeremiah confesses on behalf of the nation, including himself. He admits the people's sins are a witness for the prosecution — their own conscience condemns them. He pleads not on the basis of their worthiness but on God's character ("for Your name's sake"). "Do thou it" (KJV) means "act gloriously, intervene." (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/14.htm ; bible.org: search result summary)

- Reformed (Calvin): This is a model of true repentance. "In ourselves we find nothing but reasons for condemnation; seek then in thyself a reason for forgiving us." God must spare for His own name's sake because there is nothing in the people to compel mercy. Calvin uses this verse to refute Catholic ideas of satisfactions and works of supererogation: the only ground of forgiveness is God's own character. (Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik): Jeremiah imagines what true repentance would sound like — utter confession of guilt and appeal to pure mercy. This is the model prayer the nation should have prayed. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

**v. 8 — "O Hope of Israel, its Savior in times of distress, why are You like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who stays but a night?"**

- Traditional: The appeal is to God's covenant promises, not to Israel's fading faith. A traveler staying one night has little care for the land — but God had promised to dwell permanently among His people (2 Chronicles 33:7-8). The question presses God: why does He seem indifferent? (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Baptist (Garner-Howes): Jeremiah pleads for God to maintain the honor of His holy name as the covenant-God of Israel. Surely God cannot manifest such indifference as might be expected from a stranger merely passing through! (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

**v. 9 — "Why are You like a man taken by surprise, like a warrior powerless to save? Yet You are among us… Do not forsake us!"**

- Traditional: The image is of a mighty warrior suddenly stunned or dismayed, unable to help — a shocking picture since God is all-powerful (Isaiah 59:1). Yet the prophet reminds God that He dwells in their midst (the sanctuary) and they are "called by Your name." (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Baptist (Garner-Howes): The appeal is that failure to act will diminish God's reputation among the heathen. Since God dwells in the midst of this covenant people, His honor is at stake. (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

---

## Jeremiah 14:10-12 — God's Response: Rejection

**v. 10 — "Truly they love to wander; they have not restrained their feet. So the LORD does not accept them; He will now remember their guilt…"**

- Traditional: The imagined repentance of vv.7-9 was just that — imagination. The real Judah "loved to wander" after idols and never restrained themselves. Therefore God "does not accept them." The verse quotes Hosea 8:13 almost verbatim. The emphasis on "now" indicates the time of judgment has arrived — when iniquity is fully ripe. (Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/ ; JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Reformed (Ligonier): God's reply is "shocking in its harsh statements." The people loved to wander and refused to turn back. Their repentance was only in Jeremiah's prophetic imagination, not in reality. (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/false-promise-peace)

**v. 11 — "Do not pray for the well-being of this people"**

- Traditional: This is the third time God forbids Jeremiah to pray for Judah (cf. Jeremiah 7:16; 11:14). The people have passed a point of no return; their course is set. Yet the very command assumes Jeremiah WOULD pray — an evidence of his intercessory heart. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

- Reformed (Ligonier): "Surely the nation had passed the point of no return if He was unwilling to hear the prayers of the prophets appointed to intercede for His people." Yet astonishingly, Jeremiah did not heed the charge — he prayed anyway — and this was not sin. Prophetic oracles often use hyperbole to make the reality of judgment clear. The same God who told Jeremiah not to pray also said He relents when a nation turns from sin (Jeremiah 18:7-8). (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/false-promise-peace)

- Spurgeon (Baptist): "O, how dreadful is the state of that people in reference to whom the Lord says to his ministers, Pray not for them." Yet Jeremiah "edges his way up towards the throne of grace and, at last, he does what he is told not to do." (Quoted in Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/ ; Spurgeon sermon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/intercession-and-supplication)

**v. 12 — "Although they may fast, I will not listen… offer burnt offerings… I will not accept them… I will finish them off by sword and famine and plague"**

- Traditional: Even the appointed religious duties — fasting, burnt offerings, grain offerings — are rejected because they are hypocritical. The heart remains idolatrous. God never refuses real prayer, but He refuses insincere ritual. Sword, famine, and pestilence are the three standard scourges of covenant judgment. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

---

## Jeremiah 14:13-16 — False Prophets Condemned

**v. 13 — "Ah, Lord GOD! … the prophets are telling them, 'You will not see the sword or suffer famine, but I will give you lasting peace in this place'"**

- Traditional: Jeremiah attempts to excuse the people — they have been misled by false prophets who promise "peace of truth" (assured, lasting peace). This was a genuine covenant promise, but it had conditions the nation had hopelessly violated. Jeremiah's appeal is compassionate but misplaced — the people are still responsible for their own choices (cf. Deuteronomy 13:1-5; 18:22). (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; bible.org search result; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

**v. 14 — "The prophets are prophesying lies in My name… I did not send them… a false vision, a worthless divination, the futility and delusion of their own minds"**

- Traditional: Four sources of their false message are enumerated: (1) a false vision (a disordered fancy), (2) divination by signs and auguries, (3) "a thing of nought" (possibly referring to idols/teraphim used for divination), (4) the deceit of their own heart — pure imposture. God explicitly disowns them: He did not send, command, or speak to them. (Ellicott, quoted in search results: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/14.htm ; JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Reformed (Calvin): "'In my name' is emphatical." God reminds us that we must exercise judgment about prophecies — not everything boasted as divine is so. Calvin applies this against the Papists of his day: "they vainly boast of their titles, and say that they are the real Church… thus they astonish and confound the simple, so that every discrimination is taken away." (Calvin: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Baptist (Garner-Howes): Deception by false prophets is just as serious today; the man of God must be sure he is proclaiming THE WORD OF GOD, not the philosophies or wishes of men (citing Matthew 7:15; 24:11, 24; 2 Peter 2:1; 1 John 4:1). (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

**v. 15 — "By sword and famine these very prophets will meet their end!"**

- Traditional: A just retribution in kind — the very calamities they denied would come will consume them. The judgment fits the crime exactly. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

**v. 16 — "The people… will be thrown into the streets… no one to bury them… I will pour out their own evil upon them"**

- Traditional: Both deceiver and deceived are held responsible. The people "wanted to be deceived" (Jeremiah 5:31), so judgment falls on all alike. Having no burial was a special disgrace in the ancient Near East (cf. Psalm 79:3). "Pour their wickedness upon them" means the punishment their wickedness incurred. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

## Jeremiah 14:17-18 — The Lament

**v. 17 — "My eyes overflow with tears; day and night they do not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people has been shattered…"**

- Traditional: It is debated whether the speaker is Jeremiah or God (or both). "Virgin daughter" describes Judah as one who had been jealously kept from idolatrous nations, like a virgin guarded in an Oriental household — now shattered. Jeremiah is told to weep ceaselessly; he takes no satisfaction in being proven right. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/ ; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

**v. 18 — "If I go out to the country, I see those slain by the sword; if I enter the city, I see those ravaged by famine! For both prophet and priest travel to a land they do not know"**

- Traditional: No escape anywhere — field or city, sword or famine. "Prophet and priest go about in a land they do not know" — JFB suggests two possible readings: (1) they shall go into exile in a strange land, or (2) they go "trafficking about the land" (commercializing their religious office) and take no notice of the miseries before them. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

---

## Jeremiah 14:19-22 — Final Plea

**v. 19 — "Have You rejected Judah completely? Do You despise Zion? Why have You stricken us so that we are beyond healing? We hoped for peace, but no good has come… only terror"**

- Traditional: Jeremiah is astonished — has God utterly cast off His people? The people "looked for peace" because the false prophets promised it, but found only trouble. The questions grow more intense than in vv.7-9, reflecting growing desperation. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

- Baptist (Garner-Howes): Jeremiah is "astounded" that Jehovah should reject, loathe and smite His people when they looked for healing and peace (cf. Jeremiah 30:12-15; 8:15; 1 Thessalonians 5:3). (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

**v. 20 — "We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, the guilt of our fathers; indeed, we have sinned against You"**

- Traditional: A full, corporate confession — their own sins and those of previous generations (cf. Daniel 9:8). This is what God desired from the drought. Yet Adam Clarke notes: "This the prophet did in behalf of the people; but, alas! They did not join him." Harrison says Jeremiah confesses "vicariously" since the nation will not. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/ ; JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Spurgeon (Baptist): "Make a clean breast of it, unbosom the past, lay bare the present. Think not to cloak sin. To conceal sin is to ruin yourself; to confess it, is to find mercy." (Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-drought-of-nature-the-rain-of-grace-and-the-lesson-therefrom)

**v. 21 — "For the sake of Your name do not despise us; do not disgrace Your glorious throne. Remember Your covenant with us; do not break it"**

- Traditional: A three-fold basis for appeal: (1) God's name and reputation, (2) God's throne of glory — Jerusalem and the temple (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:5), and (3) God's covenant (Psalm 106:45). This anticipates New Covenant reasoning — appealing to who God is, not who we are. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/ ; Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

- Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik): "This ground of reasoning anticipates the New Covenant. Under the New Covenant we believe God for help and blessing and favor not based upon who we are or what we have done, but upon who God is and what He has done." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-14/)

**v. 22 — "Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain? Do the skies alone send showers? Is this not by You, O LORD our God? So we put our hope in You, for You have done all these things"**

- Traditional: The chapter comes full circle to the drought. "Vanities" are the idols (Deuteronomy 32:21). The rhetorical question exposes Baal-worship: Baal was the supposed storm-god, yet he is powerless. Not even the heavens themselves can give rain apart from God (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). "Therefore we will wait upon thee" — the humbled heart simply looks to God in patient reliance. (JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm ; Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/14.htm ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Baptist (Garner-Howes): Judah had constantly given credit to Baal (a storm-god) for rain and fertility rather than recognizing these as blessings from Jehovah (Jeremiah 5:24; Hosea 2:5, 8). Jeremiah confesses for the nation, but unfortunately "he spoke ONLY FOR HIMSELF: this was NOT the mind or attitude of the nation; thus, they MUST BE PUNISHED." (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-14.html)

- Reformed (Calvin): Calvin favors the reading: "Not even the heavens themselves can give rain, much less can the idol vanities." The disjunctive "or" supports this — the heavens are not the First Cause and ought not to be deified by the heathen. (JFB summary of Calvin: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/14.htm)

- Spurgeon (Baptist): "Every road is closed but the way of sovereign grace. You have no merit, you have no strength… God must save you, or you are lost to all eternity." The only refuge is in God as He reveals Himself in Christ. "Therefore we will wait upon thee." (Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-drought-of-nature-the-rain-of-grace-and-the-lesson-therefrom)

---

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

**Reformed vs. Arminian/Wesleyan on God's "relenting":** The Reformed sources (Calvin, Ligonier) stress God's sovereign decree — the drought is unstoppable judgment from a God who "restrains" nature at will. The Ligonier article, however, balances this by noting that even the harshest prophetic oracles contain hyperbole and that God "relents when a nation…turns from sin" (Jeremiah 18:7-8). I was unable to locate specific Wesleyan/Methodist commentary on this chapter from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu to compare with the Reformed view.

**Lutheran perspective:** I was unable to access Kretzmann's full commentary directly, but search excerpts indicate he reads the chapter as a unified message where God uses drought as covenant discipline (Deuteronomy 28:23), and the "false prophets" are condemned for offering "peace of truth" without repentance. No distinctively Lutheran doctrinal emphasis emerged from the available material.

**Baptist emphasis on individual responsibility:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary uniquely stresses that while false prophets misled the people, "since the people want to be deceived, judgment will fall upon deceiver and deceived alike" — an emphasis on individual accountability consistent with Baptist theology. It also applies the warning directly to contemporary preaching: "the man of God must be sure that He is proclaiming THE WORD OF GOD — not the philosophies or wishes of men."

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** David Guzik emphasizes the emotional and devotional dimensions — Jeremiah's tears, his inability to stop interceding despite God's prohibition, and the appeal to God's character over human merit. The application stresses grief over judgment and patient waiting on God. No distinctively Pentecostal doctrinal emphasis (e.g., on spiritual gifts or healing) appears in this chapter's treatment.

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to search newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for this chapter due to reaching search limits. No Catholic or Orthodox commentary on Jeremiah 14 can be reported from the available sources.

**Modern scholarship:** I could not access bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the fetch limits. Search excerpts from bible.org (an evangelical academic site) note structural observations: the chapter contains a liturgical pattern — the prayer of vv.7-9 is matched by a more intense prayer in vv.19-22, possibly reflecting temple liturgy. bible.org also notes that v.13 shows Jeremiah attempting "to blame the people's religious apostasy on the religious leaders," but that the people remain responsible for their own acts (cf. Ezekiel 18). (bible.org search result)

**Debated modern teachings:** I found no material from the allowed sources discussing prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace interpretations of this chapter.
